title: Boundary value analysis: testing the edges
summary: BVA refines equivalence partitioning for numbers: test both sides of every boundary, because off-by-one faults live exactly there.

sections.heading: Introduction
paras: Boundary value analysis (BVA) is equivalence partitioning with a magnifying glass, and it only applies to numerical inputs. Look at the borders between categories: a boundary is one step away from a different category, and a boundary value is a value sitting exactly on that edge.

Boundaries matter because programmers constantly make off-by-one faults: writing > when they meant >=, forgetting a -1 or +1, or initialising a counter to 1 instead of 0. A test in the middle of a category sails past these; a test on the edge catches them.

sections.heading: Worked example: discount
paras: The discount submodule maps item counts to rates: 0-2 items earn 0, 3-8 earn 0.15, 9+ earn 0.25, and invalid counts earn -1.0. Draw the number line and the boundaries appear between invalid and 0%, between 0% and 15%, and between 15% and 25%. Because a fault could push the error to either side, every boundary contributes two test values, one from each neighbouring category.

sections.heading: Boundaries with real numbers
paras: With integers the two values around a boundary are obvious neighbours. With reals you must pick values as close to the edge as possible: for the rule aircon on at 25.5 degrees or above, test exactly 25.5 from one side and something like 25.499999 from the other.
The pattern is always the same: find every boundary between categories, then take one value from each side. Three boundaries in the discount example mean six test values, not three.

callout.text: BVA questions expect two values per boundary with a short justification (fault could lie on either side). State the number line, name each boundary, then list the pairs; half marks are lost by giving only one value per boundary.

recall.q: When does BVA apply, and what does each boundary produce?
recall.a: BVA applies to numerical ranges. Each boundary between two categories produces two test values, one from each side, because an off-by-one fault could fail in either direction.

recall.q: Why do faults cluster at boundaries?
recall.a: Because of off-by-one mistakes: > vs >=, a missing -1 or +1, or a counter started at 1 instead of 0. Middle-of-category values pass despite these; edge values expose them.

recall.q: How do you test a real-valued boundary such as >= 25.5?
recall.a: Test the exact edge value 25.5 from one category and the closest representable neighbour (e.g. 25.499999) from the other, one value per side.

activities.prompt: Why do faults cluster at boundaries?
options: Edge inputs are exercised less often in practice

distractor.1: Frequency of use does not cause the faults — off-by-one logic does.
distractor.2: Middles pass even with off-by-one faults; only edge values expose them.
distractor.3: Tests should cover the middle too, but edges catch more.
